summary: This document explains how a sender using UDP Options can run Datagram Packetization Layer Path MTU Discovery (DPLPMTUD). The method lets an application find the largest datagram size that will cross a network path.

eli5.summary: Before mailing a big package, you want to know the largest box the postal route allows. This explains how to test sizes until you find the biggest one that fits.

questions: what is dplpmtud for udp options
how does udp path mtu discovery work
what are the req and res options in udp
why use a random token in udp probes
subtitle: How a UDP sender uses the REQ and RES options to find the largest datagram a path will carry.

tldr.problem: UDP gives applications no automatic way to learn the largest datagram that crosses a path without IP fragmentation, and ICMP Packet Too Big messages are sometimes dropped.
tldr.mechanism: The sender pads probe packets to a chosen size and attaches a REQ option with a 4-byte token; the receiver echoes the token in a RES option, proving a packet of that size got through.
tldr.outcome: The result is a robust search for the largest packet size, repeated to check the path still works, that does not depend on ICMP and needs support at both ends.

facts.label: RES rate limit example
facts.value: 1 per measured RTT or 1 per second per pair of ports

facts.label: Probe fragmentation
facts.value: MUST NOT be fragmented; DF bit set in IPv4

today: RFC 9869 is a Proposed Standard published in October 2025 and has not been obsoleted. It depends on the UDP Options defined in RFC 9868 and on the generic method in RFC 8899.

sections.title: Why Probe the Path
sections.content:
UDP Usage Guidelines (RFC 8085) say an application SHOULD use path MTU information from the IP layer or run Path MTU Discovery itself, to avoid IP fragments. The UDP API offers no automatic way to find the supported size. RFC 8899 defines Datagram Packetization Layer PMTUD (DPLPMTUD) for datagram transports, a probing method that does not rely only on ICMP Packet Too Big (PTB) messages and so works on paths that drop them.

RFC 9869 says how to run DPLPMTUD with the UDP Options of RFC 9868. Doing it in the transport service saves each upper layer protocol from implementing the method. It needs support enabled at both sender and receiver. If multipath or multihoming is used, each path needs its own state machine. DPLPMTUD is not specified for multicast.
sections.eli5: It is like testing which size of box fits through a mail slot. You try bigger and bigger boxes and ask the person inside to shout back each time one arrives.

sections.title: How DPLPMTUD Uses UDP Options
sections.content:
DPLPMTUD here is built from a pair of options: the Request (REQ) option and the Response (RES) option, plus the End of Options List (EOL) option to pad a probe to the wanted size. Use MUST be explicitly enabled by the application, and a receiver MUST NOT answer a REQ until DPLPMTUD is enabled, to guard against misuse of the mechanism for other forms of probing. By default the API MUST disable it.

It can live in the UDP transport service or in an upper layer protocol or application. When it lives in the transport, the state machine sends the probes and finds the PLPMTU, which fixes the Maximum Packet Size (MPS). The discovered size can set the maximum datagram size or the maximum fragment size when the UDP Fragmentation option is used. If it runs at more than one layer, the tokens must be coordinated so each probe is identifiable, and the RFC advises avoiding discovery at both levels.

Probes sent with no payload were not generated by an application, so the receiver does not deliver them to its application.
sections.eli5: One side asks "can you hear me?" with a numbered card, and the other side holds the same card up in reply. The size of the shout is what is being tested.

sections.title: Probe Packets and Tokens
sections.content:
A probe packet carries a UDP Options area with a REQ option and any other needed options, ended by EOL, then padding up to the probe size. A probe can be as large as the local interface MTU, and its size MUST NOT be constrained by a smaller path MTU learned from network layer mechanisms. Probes MUST NOT be fragmented at the UDP or IP layer, and in IPv4 they MUST be sent with the Don't Fragment (DF) bit set.

The token is four bytes. Each probe MUST be uniquely identifiable within the Maximum Segment Lifetime, and a sender MUST NOT reuse a token in that time. It needs to be unique only for the specific 5-tuple. The first value SHOULD be randomized, to protect against off-path attacks. A RES echoes the last received token.

If a responder sends a datagram solely to carry a RES, it MUST rate limit these responses, for example one per measured RTT or one per second for each pair of ports. This reduces the denial of service risk without noticeably affecting DPLPMTUD.
sections.eli5: Every question card gets its own random number so nobody can fake a reply, and you never reuse a number too soon. A helper is not allowed to answer too fast or too often.

sections.title: Sender Procedures
sections.content:
There are three kinds of probe. To confirm connectivity, UDP has no mechanism of its own, so a sender MUST send a probe padded to BASE_PLPMTU with a REQ option; a matching RES confirms a packet of that size crossed the path and that the remote end supports RES. To search for a larger size, DPLPMTUD enters the SEARCHING state, for instance after the PMTU_RAISE_TIMER expires. A Maximum Datagram Size (MDS) option from the remote end MAY be used as a hint. These probes SHOULD NOT carry application data, because they are lost whenever they exceed the real PMTU, and they MUST include REQ.

To validate the path, the sender MUST check that the discovered PLPMTU still works, by sending probes of that size with a REQ in the SEARCH_COMPLETE state to detect black holes. A probe used to confirm connectivity or validate the path MAY carry application data, such as an upper layer control message that need not be delivered reliably. In that case the receiver MUST process the REQ and return the RES with an upper layer message. A simple implementation can use only padding probes without application data, which avoids retransmitting data when a probe fails.
sections.eli5: First check that a small box gets through at all. Then try bigger boxes now and then. Later, resend a box of the size you picked to make sure the route has not shrunk.

sections.title: Network Events and PTB Messages
sections.content:
The method does not depend on events from the network, but it can use them. A change in the path or a lost probe can make DPLPMTUD update the PLPMTU. A path change notification can trigger path validation, and an upper layer can trigger validation when it sees a high packet loss rate or repeated timeouts. Implementations sharing PLPMTU between layers, for example through the IP cache, must be robust to varied forwarding behavior.

Support for ICMP PTB messages is OPTIONAL, so a sender can ignore them. Before using one, DPLPMTUD must check that it answers a probe the sender really sent. The receiver MUST validate the protocol information in the quoted packet, and SHOULD confirm that the token in the quoted REQ option matches a recently sent probe. An implementation that cannot do this validation MUST ignore received PTB messages.
sections.eli5: Sometimes a postal worker sends a note saying "too big." You only believe it if the note quotes your own numbered card, because anyone could write a fake note.

sections.title: Different Receiver Behaviors
sections.content:
The RFC lists four cases that show how the receiver's behavior changes the result.

  • No receiver support: no RES is ever received, so the PLPMTU cannot be discovered and the minimum configured PLPMTU (MIN_PLPMTU) is used.
  • Receiver replies with application datagrams: the RES goes out with the next datagram sent back. This works with traffic in both directions and avoids opportunities for DoS misuse, but a low return rate delays the RES and can leave a smaller PLPMTU than the path supports.
  • Unidirectional transfer: waiting for a queued datagram can easily cause a probe timeout, so exchanging datagrams without a payload could be allowed to return the RES.
  • Receiver may send payload-free responses: this ensures timely progress but could let others probe which UDP ports support the specification, so the rate limit from the previous section applies.
sections.eli5: Some helpers shout back right away, some only reply when they were going to write you anyway, and some never reply. The less a helper answers, the less sure you are about the biggest box.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The security considerations of RFC 9868 and RFC 8899 apply, and the method does not change the integrity protection offered by UDP Options. On-path attackers could drop or modify probes to try to lower the PMTU or black-hole traffic.

A token that is easy to guess, such as an incremented value, would let an on-path observer work out later tokens and forge probes, so the first value is randomized and an unpredictable token per probe is a mitigation. A sender using PTB messages MUST validate the quoted UDP ports together with the token. Upper layer protocols that use encryption ought to run DPLPMTUD above UDP Options instead, so probes are encrypted and the application controls the extra traffic. The RFC has no IANA actions.
sections.eli5: If your question cards are numbered 1, 2, 3, a sneaky watcher can guess the next one and send fake replies. Random numbers make that guessing much harder.
